A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same feature-flow and model-steering work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–F are readable and support reliable matching despite pagination and figure-number changes.

before.justification: v1 reports original feature-predecessor identification, causal deactivation, thematic steering, and SAE transition experiments in Section 5 and the appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds Pearson-correlation matching and exhaustive-search comparisons in Section 5.2 and Appendix C.4.

M1.justification: Cosine-based feature matching, flow-graph construction, and steering procedures remain unchanged. The intervention formula and steering strategies expanded in Section 4.2 were already documented in v1's Appendices A–B. Pearson matching and exhaustive search are evaluation comparators, not new proposed components.

E1.justification: Both versions use FineWeb, TinyStories, AutoMathText, PythonGithubCode, and the same thematic steering tasks. The added correlation comparison reuses existing input domains; its additional models and sampling procedures change experimental settings rather than dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds an evaluated top-1 Pearson-correlation comparator for predecessor identification and deactivation, plus an exhaustive-search reference for deactivation (Table 1 and Appendix C.4). These substantially extend comparisons supporting the central matching approach. The original random, permutation, top-5, and steering comparisons remain.

E3.justification: Appendix C.4 introduces correlation estimation using 100K non-special FineWeb tokens, 500-sample grouping, Gemma even layers, and all layers of Pythia-70M-Deduped and GPT-2. The new deactivation comparison tests the same 1,894 targets across two layers, restricted to single-module predecessor groups identified by either matcher. These are additional protocols; Appendix A's original 250-sample identification study remains unchanged.

E4.justification: The new exhaustive-search experiment investigates how much causal deactivation effectiveness the matching methods miss. Appendix C.4 also examines matching agreement, attention-predecessor identification, and dataset dependence, including Python code after FineWeb-based correlation estimation. These add substantive validation questions beyond the retained rescaling, steering, and transition-map analyses.

E5.justification: The Mann–Whitney U-test procedure and p < 0.001 threshold are retained, as are existing plotted uncertainty displays. The new comparisons add no repeated-run or seed information, confidence intervals, or significance tests; their sample sizes describe evaluation design.

E6.justification: New Table 1 reports mean activation change/success rate of 0.75/65% for cosine matching, 0.74/65% for Pearson matching, and 0.83/73% for exhaustive search. Figure 18 and Appendix C.4 add comparative feature-group distributions and qualitative Pythia/GPT-2 findings. These are substantive new results under additional protocols; matched pre-existing results remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The linear-representation assumptions, matching definitions, transformation equations, and Appendix F's relationship between matching and transcoders are retained. Restating the existing intervention formula in the main text adds explanation, not new mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's three contributions, and Section 8 retain the same claims about data-free cross-layer mapping, circuit interpretation, and multi-layer steering. The added comparator results support these contributions without redefining their central scope or novelty.

C2.justification: v3 discusses correlation matching's dataset dependence, sparse-feature difficulties, and possible attention-SAE misalignment. Section 5.3 qualifies cumulative steering's advantage to a low-r regime, and Section 6 clarifies why module-level removal may fail when a feature persists in the residual stream. Existing broader limitations remain.

D1.justification: The new experiments document the FineWeb subset, non-special-token filtering, model/layer selection, and exhaustive-search eligibility and intervention procedure. Existing SAE and steering details in Appendices A–B are retained; their expanded main-text explanation is not newly disclosed information.

R1.justification: v3 adds Gao et al., Scaling and evaluating sparse autoencoders, to the Top-K discussion and modestly strengthens positioning against data-driven matching. Several existing references receive publication or title updates, which do not constitute additional works. The related-work section's principal positioning remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Section 4.2 is expanded using existing appendix material, portions of the results and discussion are rewritten, and Appendix C.4 is added. The overall narrative structure remains stable. v3 also updates an author affiliation and conference text and replaces the erroneous submission-template running header.

P2.justification: v3 adds Table 1 and Figure 18, swaps the ordering of the two deactivation-analysis figures, and relocates several existing displays. Figure 10's caption is clarified. Existing graphics and feature tables are retained, with limited layout adjustments rather than a broad visual redesign.

improvement.justification: v3 improves validation by directly comparing cosine matching with Pearson matching and an exhaustive-search reference, addressing an important comparison missing from v1. It also qualifies the steering interpretation and improves presentation. The gain remains limited: the new causal comparison covers selected groups on two layers without uncertainty estimates, and the additional model findings are documented briefly.
